# The Mirror and the Authority

The obvious objection arrives immediately. The enterprise already has a Git
host. It is reliable, it is familiar, it is somebody else's operational
problem, and the canon already lives on it today. Why stand up a Windows
server to do what a SaaS platform does better and cheaper? The objection is
reasonable, and the answer is not that the SaaS platform is bad. The answer
is that a mirror and an authority are different roles, and the boundary does
not let the same system play both.

A mirror is where canon is ingested. It is a convenience, a collaboration
surface, a place where the wider world can read and propose. Public-internet
Git hosting is excellent at this, and nothing in this book argues against
keeping it. An authority is something else. It is where canon is decided —
where a commit becomes binding, where a webhook fires that recalculates a
group, where a server-side hook either accepts or rejects a change to the
governance corpus. The authority is not a place you read from; it is the
place the rest of the substrate obeys. And the moment a system has that kind
of power over governance, it inherits every constraint that governance is
subject to.

The cloud boundary for the program is GCC-Moderate, and the discipline of a
boundary is that it does not bend for convenience. Every commit, every
webhook, every audit record produced by the authority of record must sit
under the same authorization plane that governs the rest of the substrate.
If the directory, the policy engine, and the telemetry pipeline all live
inside the boundary, then the system that decides what those things *are*
cannot live outside it. Otherwise the most consequential object in the
architecture — the one that defines every other object — would be governed
by a different authority than the things it governs. That is not a tidy
exception; it is a hole straight through the center of the model.

So the relationship inverts cleanly. The public host upstream is the source
of canon *ingest*: a pull-mirror keeps the on-premises instance current with
the wider world on a short interval, and contributors who live outside the
boundary still have a place to work. The on-premises instance is the source
of canon *authority*: it is the one whose history is binding, whose hooks are
enforced, whose audit log an assessor will eventually read. There is no
inbound path from the public internet to the authority. The mirror flows in;
authority does not flow out.

This is the decision recorded in the architecture: keep the convenience of
the cloud as a mirror, but place the authority of record where the boundary
requires it. Having established *that* it must live inside, the next question
is *how many* of it there should be — and the answer is more pointed than it
first appears.
